Originally Built for a Billionaire Heiress, This Rare Yacht Now Sports a Modest Price Tag
26 photos
Photo: IYC
Although not remarkably innovative in terms of engineering or interior design, this 40-meter (131 feet) yacht is special in more ways than one. It’s one of the very few Kiwi-built luxury yachts, for a short while it bore the name of a great Canadian personality, and it eventually became a rare catch as the original shipyard that had delivered it in 2009 ceased operations.
When you’re a billionaire and the heiress of an enduring media empire, you can have your pick of luxury pleasure craft. Most people in this situation choose ultra-sophisticated, behemoth-sized, and even futuristic megayachts built by the world’s top names in the superyacht industry, such as the greatest Dutch, German, or Italian shipyards. The late Loretta Ann Rogers, who passed away in 2022, went a very different route.
There were four yachts that bore her name, and all came from the same shipyard - a relatively young builder in New Zealand, with an unusual history, and sadly a short career, eventually ceasing operations in 2016. That choice is highly unusual for someone with the wealth and status of the Rogers heiress, and it makes all of these four yachts rare and special. Delivered in 2009, Vesper is the one that flaunted this name for a short while, but it’s no less unique than the others.
The fact that Loretta Ann Rogers chose to commission these pleasure craft throughout the years indicates her close bond, described as a patronage type of relationship, with the New Zealand-based shipyard, and it certainly leaves a considerable heritage behind for this brand. AY28, and then AY32 were the first two official Loretta Ann yachts. AY32, launched in 2005, was named Ab Initio, and the AY38 (currently Vesper) that would be launched in 2009 was based on it.
Photo: IYC According to the builder himself, AY38 was only a placeholder while the bigger AY43 was under construction. That is why AY38, launched as Allogante, quickly changed its name to Loretta Ann IV, but then “transferred” this name to the AY43, once that was completed and delivered. The AY43 (most recently known as Ab Initio) was, at 47 meters (154 feet) the largest Alloy Yachts build.
The builder referred to the Rogers heiress as “a noted philanthropist, talented artist, environmentalist and compassionate superyacht owner” and indicated that this final yacht, the AY43, also reflected “the culmination of years of ownership experience”.
Loretta Ann and her four children had all inherited a large stake in Roger Communications, after Ted Rogers passed away in 2008. This telecoms and media empire provides cable TV, telephone, and internet services, and it also owns Canada's largest publisher, Rogers Publishing.
Early on, the Rogers family was also recognized for its philanthropy. In 2014, the Rogers $130 million donation to establish the Ted Rogers Centre for Heart Research became the largest single donation in the history of Canadian health care. Loretta also founded the Loretta A. Rogers Chair in Eating Disorders at Toronto General & Western Hospital.
Photo: IYC Originally named Allogante, Vesper was launched in 2009. At the time, it was described as a development of the 2005 Ad Lib (another one of the Loretta Ann yachts mentioned prior), incorporating all of its signature features, but also boasting the best technical upgrades available. Like most luxury motor yachts by Alloy Yachts, it was the result of a collaboration between Dubois Naval Architects and Donald Starkey (for the interior design).
After its 2009 debut, this 40-meter yacht changed hands quite a few times. The original launch name was Allogante, then it was named Loretta Ann while it served as a placeholder for her bigger yacht. Over the years, it was also known as Tat’s, So Nice, and is currently back on the market as Vesper.
Although not necessarily innovative or outstanding in terms of style, Vesper is remarkable for its size category. That’s mainly because it offers an unusual amount of outdoor space, similar to a much bigger yacht. Plus, it offers the benefit of a shallow draft (2.3 meters/7.5 feet) that allows it to access bays that are forbidden for yachts of the same length, but larger.
This was an important requirement for the late heiress, as the larger Loretta Ann (47 meters) also had a shallow draft specifically for easy access to the Bahamas and Belize.
Photo: IYC All Alloy Yachts motor yacht share the distinctive deep navy blue hull color that makes them easily recognizable, along with a modern, angular silhouette that hints at a sporty performance. Vesper flaunts the same signature look, and its smart, flexible layout can be described as a heaven for extended vacations on the water. Its unusually large sun deck is basically an entire floor of the yacht that offers a jacuzzi, a bar, shaded al-fresco dining and BBQ, all on one level.
The jacuzzi is placed aft, surrounded by sun loungers and in proximity to a full bar. The barbecue station added here means that the crew don’t have to waste time moving between the galley and the sun deck, since everything can be prepared right there, on deck. The foredeck reveals another sun lounging area, with an unusual hammock swing (rigged off the side deck) added for relaxation.
The main deck aft is also somewhat unusual because of its high flexibility. It was purposely designed to switch easily between a dining setup with a generously-sized table for lunch, and a cocktail setup with a low coffee table and cozy sofas all around. In addition to that, the classic dining area is easily accessed from the salon on the main deck, and it even comes with a full-stocked wine gallery.
In terms of accommodation, a total of five cabins can welcome up to 12 guests, plus separate quarters for a crew of seven. The master suite enjoys the best placement (forward on the main deck) and it has enough floor space for a separate study and a walk-in wardrobe. All the other four cabins are on the lower deck, and they include a twin cabin with Pullman berths for added flexibility.
Photo: IYC The side-opening tender garage, which doubles as a water-level gym, houses a big (16.6 feet) Williams Dieseljet tender and dive compressor. Two more personal watercraft (PWCs) are stored on the foredeck, and can be handled using the dedicated deck crane.
Built to Lloyd’s classification and constantly well-maintained, Vesper enjoyed a successful charter career over the years, with weekly rates in the Mediterranean starting at €126,000. It was most recently refitted in Spain in 2025, and is currently asking for €10,9 million ($12.2 million).
Vesper is not only one of the few yachts that were owned and named after one of the greatest contemporary philanthropists, but also a rare Kiwi yacht. Alloy Yachts, the New Zealand-based builder, brought to life some of the best sailing yachts of the ‘90s, including the 159-foot sloop Georgia, which became the world’s largest single-mast sailing yacht at the time.
Photo: IYC Sadly, because the demand for sailing yachts dropped dramatically, and because of challenging economic times for New Zealand’s exporters, Allow Yachts decided to end its operations in 2016. This means that there is a limited number of Alloy Yachts pleasure craft still out there, and there will never be a new one (at least, not in the foreseeable future). Vesper is a collector’s item for this reason alone, and valuable beyond its $12 million price tag.
